abstract: This conceptual paper argues that the popular but ill-defined metaphors of 'echo chambers' and 'filter bubbles' should be replaced by a feedback-loop perspective on communication in the digital society. It reconciles two seemingly contradictory observations—the lack of empirical evidence for pervasive bubbles and the real existence of self-reinforcing, sometimes harmful, communicative dynamics—by showing that feedback loops can reinforce processes without producing catastrophic, inevitable radicalization. The author develops a typology of communicative feedback loops, applies it to contemporary problems, and proposes concrete empirical methods for studying them.
key_claims: Echo chamber and filter bubble metaphors are vague and empirically contested, yet contain a kernel of truth about reinforcing selection processes; a feedback-loop perspective offers a better theoretical foundation.

A feedback-loop perspective explains why self-reinforcing processes do not inevitably produce full radicalization, resolving the paradox that filter-bubble/echo-chamber models predict rapid radicalization that has not become omnipresent.
Communicative feedback loops cannot be modeled as linear relationships over time (Proposition 1); once reinforcing relationships reach extremes, they break or reverse.
Both reinforcing (positive) and self-regulating (negative) feedback loops exist, and they coexist with exogenous forces within a complex system that is never fully closed.
Algorithmic communicative feedback loops tend toward an equilibrium rather than the extremes (Proposition 2), because recommender systems and user behavior both correct overly narrow personalization.
In digital environments with multiple feedback loops, emergent system-level behavior often cannot be inferred from the individual components alone (Proposition 3).
methods: Conceptual and theoretical synthesis drawing on cybernetics, systems theory, complexity science, and computational social science.
Development of a typology (Table 1) distinguishing within-human, between-human, human–algorithm, and pure algorithmic feedback loops, mapped to relevant theoretical foundations.
Review and integration of prior empirical literature on recommender systems, misinformation spread, radicalization, and gatekeeping.

Proposal and comparison (Table 2) of empirical approaches for studying feedback loops: agent-based modeling/simulation, algorithm audits and agent-based testing (sock puppets), experience sampling method (ESM), data donation, and online field experiments.
Argument for shifting research designs from 'large N, small T' toward 'small N, large T' to capture temporal dynamics of feedback loops.
findings: Contemporary recommender systems introduce randomness, serendipity, and diversity, and users correct systems by clicking non-recommended items, producing negative feedback loops (analogous to a thermostat) rather than runaway personalization.
YouTube has been shown to recommend increasingly extreme content (Ribeiro et al.; Kaiser & Rauchfleisch), but similar loops were not found on Reddit and Gab (Whittaker et al.).

Mis- and disinformation spread partly because mainstream media attention—even critical—amplifies it, so it travels beyond partisan in-groups rather than remaining confined to a bubble (Proposition 4).

Fringe groups have incentives to express and exaggerate radical positions to gain newsworthiness, creating feedback loops that drive further radicalization ('fringe bubbles', 'vicious cycle of counterpublics') (Proposition 5).
Benkler et al. found self-correcting feedback loops in left-wing and non-partisan US media but positive, escalating loops in right-wing media.
Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) explicitly forbid cycles, so standard causal-inference frameworks are inadequate for studying feedback loops, motivating alternative empirical strategies.
contributions: Reframes echo chamber/filter bubble debates through an integrative feedback-loop lens that renders these metaphors 'moot' while preserving their valid concerns.
Provides a novel typology of communicative feedback loops bridging (social-)psychological, sociological, and computer-science literatures that are otherwise disjointed.
Offers five testable propositions to guide a research agenda on feedback loops in digital communication.

Maps a practical methodological toolbox (with references to open-source tools such as ScrapeBot, OSD2F, PORT, CART, and the 3bij3 news app) so researchers can study feedback loops without requiring massive datasets or computing resources.

Argues that ecologically valid, messy research designs combining multiple methods (e.g., shareworthiness studies plus algorithm audits plus simulation) can disentangle intertwined human and algorithmic contributions.
framing: The paper positions itself within communication science and computational social science, drawing on cybernetics, systems theory, and complexity/emergence traditions (Ashby, Slater's reinforcing spiral model, the dynamic-transactional approach, gatekeeping theory). It engages the ongoing scholarly debate over the reality and utility of filter bubble and echo chamber concepts, seeking to replace metaphor with dynamic, testable models of human–algorithm interaction.
